managedInterfaces.perContractNotPerClass: GraphicsDeviceManager implements BOTH IGraphicsDeviceService and IGraphicsDeviceManager. internalXNAInterfaces.exhaustive: declared like the BCL set; an XNA interface that is neither a public contract type nor declared internal is INTERFACE_MAPPING_MISMATCH

events.handler: System.EventHandler<T> -> EventHandler[T]; the generic argument is mapped exactly and never degraded to any, a bare func, a channel, or a callback word
events.handlerErrorResult: GO_LANGUAGE_PROJECTION of the CLR exception channel, never an additional XNA return identity
events.eventArgs: System.EventArgs -> *framework.EventArgs; a CLR class keeps reference semantics, so nil is not the projection of EventArgs.Empty and neither any, struct{}, nor map[string]any is admitted
events.eventArgsEmpty: System.EventArgs.Empty -> framework.EventArgsEmpty(), one stable private singleton behind a function so no consumer can reassign the shared identity
events.accessorPair: one CLR event -> exactly two projected Go accessors, unchanged from the settled rule
events.subscriptionIdentity: GO_LANGUAGE_PROJECTION: Go func values are not comparable, so a token names the registration rather than the handler; adding one handler twice yields two registrations and two tokens, unlike CLR Delegate.Remove identity matching
events.nilHandler: Add(nil) registers nothing and returns the zero token, mirroring Delegate.Combine(existing, null) returning existing
events.absentToken: the zero token, an already-removed token, and a token owned by another event all leave every registration list unchanged, mirroring Delegate.Remove of an absent delegate
events.dispatch: registration order over a snapshot taken under the lock; mutation during a raise affects later raises only
events.dispatchFailure: the first non-nil handler error propagates, no later handler runs, and the registration list survives the failure
events.lockScope: no internal lock is held while a consumer handler runs
events.supportTypes: EventSource[T] is public language support so a type declared outside CNA-Go can implement an event-bearing XNA contract; it is measured as an adapter and adds no XNA identity

bclBaseRelationships.rule: a non-XNA CLR base is a measured relationship, never exported Go embedding; Go has no CLR inheritance and embedding would promote members the XNA contract never declared
bclBaseRelationships.derivedProjection: a derived XNA class projects as its own pointer reference type
bclBaseRelationships.addsProjectedSurface: false for IMPLIED, MAPPED and DEFERRED; a COMPOSED base is the one exception and its contribution is counted as BCL_INHERITED_MEMBER_PROJECTIONS, never as an XNA-declared reference member
bclBaseRelationships.exhaustive: every non-XNA base in the profile is declared here; an undeclared base is BASE_MAPPING_MISMATCH, so no base can be dropped in silence
bclBaseRelationships.deferredMeaning: a DEFERRED base is still an open public-API decision, and no derived type may be projected until it is taken
bclBaseRelationships.composedMeaning: a COMPOSED base is a supported BCL family whose PUBLIC members remain part of the observable public CLR surface of every derived type; the derived Go type holds a PRIVATE generic adapter for the base and re-exposes those members through measured forwarding, so the surface does not disappear merely because the XNA assembly metadata does not declare it

deferredDetail.System.Attribute: ARCHITECTURE: Go has no attribute metadata, so a projected attribute type could be constructed and read back but never applied; the five ContentSerializer* types would be inert data objects whose whole purpose is unrepresentable. SUBSYSTEM: the inherited static lookups take System.Reflection Assembly/MemberInfo/Module/ParameterInfo, and whether inherited STATICS are part of a derived type's projected surface is itself undecided, having never arisen before.
deferredDetail.System.IO.BinaryReader: SUBSYSTEM: BaseStream needs a seekable System.IO.Stream; CNA-Go maps that to io.Reader, which carries neither seeking nor the encoding-aware reads the inherited surface depends on
deferredDetail.System.ComponentModel.ExpandableObjectCo: SUBSYSTEM: ITypeDescriptorContext (the profile's single largest blocker at thirteen types), System.Globalization.CultureInfo, and System.Collections.IDictionary
deferredDetail.System.Collections.ObjectModel.ReadOnlyC: DEFERRED AS A BASE ONLY; SUPPORTED as a signature adapter, and the two roles are independent. ARCHITECTURE: all four consumers declare a GetEnumerator that HIDES the inherited one, and the settled collision rule would resolve that into two hashed names; the principled answer -- a hidden inherited member is unreachable because CNA-Go projects no base type to cast to -- is available but untested. SUBSYSTEM: each consumer is blocked on its element type regardless.

bclBaseRelationships.deferredIsMeasured: a DEFERRED base must NAME what blocks it, down to the exact inherited member or the exact architecture decision, and the verifier fails a deferred base that records nothing; deferring with no recorded blocker would be an unmeasured structural category wearing a status word

blockerKinds.SUBSYSTEM: one inherited member's type belongs to a .NET subsystem CNA-Go has not mapped; the entry names both the member and the subsystem
blockerKinds.ARCHITECTURE: a cross-cutting public-API decision rather than a missing type, so no single member carries it

crossPackageCycleRule: when an ancestor namespace member returns a descendant namespace type that imports ancestor values, project the accessor as a descendant-package function named OwnerTypeMember

bclBaseAdapters.rule: a CLR class that inherits a supported BCL collection base projects as a concrete Go reference type CONTAINING a private generic adapter for that base, which re-exposes the inherited public surface through measured forwarding members
bclBaseAdapters.exportedEmbeddingIsForbidden: type X struct { Collection[T] } is refused: it publishes a Go type the contract never declares, promotes a method set the derived type never declared, implies a Go subtype relationship CLR inheritance does not create, and exposes support implementation; the verifier rejects it
bclBaseAdapters.adapterVisibility: the adapter type and the field that holds it are both unexported, and no projected signature ever names either; when a COMPOSED base gains a consumer outside the framework package the adapter moves to an internal package rather than becoming exported
bclBaseAdapters.hookArchitecture: the base's protected virtual members are projected as an UNEXPORTED Go interface, so only a type declared in this module can supply or reach a hook; every mutating public operation routes through it, so a subclass override always runs and nothing appends to the backing store and separately fakes the override's observable effect
bclBaseAdapters.storageExposure: forbidden: the backing store is never returned, never aliased into a caller's hands, and never an exported field, and a Dictionary-derived or Collection-derived type is never projected as a bare map[K]V or []T
bclBaseAdapters.behaviorAuthority: inherited behavior comes from the exact .NET Framework BCL the pinned XNA assemblies bind against, read from IL, never from modern .NET and never from Go convention; a family whose exact behavior cannot be established stays DEFERRED

System.Exception.widensAtEveryPosition: the settled substitutable-base rule widens a base-typed PARAMETER and leaves a base-typed RETURN as the concrete pointer. An exception hierarchy exists to be told apart by type, so InnerException returning a concrete *Exception would erase which of the eight kinds a consumer chained. System.Exception therefore widens at every position, and the downcast a C# consumer writes as `catch (DeviceLostException)` is a Go type assertion. The interface carries an unexported accessor, so only this module can satisfy it
System.Exception.notAGoError: a projected OPERATION reports failure through a Go error, as it has since Foundation 1, and no settled per-operation fallibility decision is reopened. A CLR exception OBJECT is a value the profile constructs and passes, and it needs a Go spelling or the members that carry it cannot be projected. Giving the type an Error() method would collapse the two and publish a member the pinned CLR type does not declare

gameBaseCallAdapters.rule: GameCallbacks projects CLR protected virtual OVERRIDES, and in CLR the override -- not the framework -- decides whether and when the base body runs. Go has no `base` keyword, so each supported override gets ONE package-level function in the framework package that runs the base body, and a callback that never calls one gets no base behavior at all
gameBaseCallAdapters.baseBehaviorIsNeverAutomatic: CNA-Go must not run a base body around a callback. Doing so would make every override a mandatory base call at a position CNA-Go picked, which is a different contract that merely resembles XNA's: omitting base.Update(t) is legal and means the component loop does not run that frame, and moving the call changes what runs before what
theseAreNot: an XNA identity: they add nothing to REFERENCE_MEMBERS, EXPECTED_GO_MEMBERS, or any type's projected member set
a member of Game: they are package-level functions so Game's projected member surface gains no name Microsoft never declared
a member of GameCallbacks: the callback contract is unchanged
a way to invoke GameCallbacks: no base body in the reference calls the virtual it is the base of, and neither does any of these
an allowlist entry: they are admitted from the measured registry, which is what subjects them to measurement
gameBaseCallAdapters.closure: the registry keys are exactly the GameCallbacks members, which are exactly the Game protected virtuals the mapper redirects. An adapter for anything else is an invented helper; a callback member without one leaves an override unable to reach its base. Both are verifier failures
gameBaseCallAdapters.firstParameter: *Game, which is the `this` a CLR base call passes implicitly
gameBaseCallAdapters.fallibility: every error result names its reasons. GUARD is the Go-only nil/unconstructed-Game check, which has no CLR counterpart and is the condition Game.Run and Game.Exit already report; REFERENCE is a failure the reference base body itself can produce. An error result with no recorded reason, and a recorded reason with no error result, are both rejected
gameBaseCallAdapters.deferredSteps: every reference step the projection does not reproduce is recorded with a class -- SUBSYSTEM, ARCHITECTURE or UNOBSERVABLE -- and a reason. A deferral marked observable from the managed component surface is REJECTED: that is a stop condition, not a deferral

xnaBaseRelationships.rule: every CLR class in the pinned profile that another class in the SAME profile inherits from is recorded here with a status. This is a different frontier from bclBaseRelationships: a BCL base is a type outside the contract that CNA-Go decides how to model, while an XNA base is a type inside the contract whose public surface a derived type inherits WITHOUT the contract redeclaring it
xnaBaseRelationships.whyItIsMeasured: Texture2D's contract declares sixteen members and inherits nine more from Texture and GraphicsResource -- Name, Tag, GraphicsDevice, IsDisposed, Dispose, ToString, Disposing, LevelCount and Format. CNA-Go projects Texture2D with none of them, and until Foundation 33 nothing recorded that. The same silence covered SpriteBatch

statuses.COMPOSED: the inheritance is projected: the base is private named state on the derived type and every inherited public member is enumerated, attributed and required. It does NOT state that any derived type is complete
statuses.DEFERRED: CNA-Go does not, and the relationship must name what blocks it

xnaBaseRelationships.deferredMustNameItsBlockers: a DEFERRED XNA base that records no blocker is a verifier failure, exactly as a DEFERRED BCL base is

blockerClasses.ARCHITECTURE: a cross-cutting projection decision no single member carries
blockerClasses.SUBSYSTEM: the base reaches a .NET or CNA subsystem CNA-Go does not map
blockerClasses.TRANSITIVE: the base is itself unprojected because its own base is deferred
blockerClasses.NATIVE_OWNERSHIP: the base is natively owned and its ownership is undecided

xnaBaseRelationships.noCompleteDerivedType: no derived type of a DEFERRED XNA base may be reported COMPLETE. Completeness asserts that a type's whole public surface is present, and the inherited half is not; a PARTIAL derived type is correct because its gap is already MISSING_MEMBER
xnaBaseRelationships.theOpenArchitectureDecision: projecting any derived XNA class needs three things CNA-Go does not have: a composition and forwarding rule for a base that is itself an XNA identity; a third provenance class beside XNA-declared and BCL-inherited so no member is counted twice; and an override adapter for the base's protected virtuals, which GameCallbacks solves for Game alone. Exported Go embedding of an XNA base is refused by BASE_MAPPING_MISMATCH and stays refused
xnaBaseRelationships.closure: the registry covers every XNA-to-XNA link the pinned contract declares -- 12 bases over 41 derived types -- so a new one cannot appear unnoticed

substitutabilityInventory.rule: before any composition rule can be called sufficient, the ACTUAL CLR substitutability requirement is measured mechanically from the pinned contract: every PUBLIC signature position -- parameter, return, property type, field type, event type, or a type named inside an array, a by-reference marker or a generic argument -- whose CLR type names a class another class in the same profile derives from
substitutabilityInventory.whyMeasuredNotArgued: the worry that private composition cannot express CLR substitutability is only real where the profile actually NAMES a base class in a public signature. If nothing takes or returns a GameComponent, no consumer can ever need a DrawableGameComponent to stand in for one. That is a counting question, and it is answered by counting

requirement.NONE: no public signature in the profile names this base, so no derived value can ever be required to stand in for one. Private named composition with explicit forwarding is not a compromise for such a family -- it is exactly sufficient, permanently, unless the pinned contract changes
requirement.LATENT: public positions name this base, but no projected carrier meets a projected derived type, so nothing can flow through one yet
requirement.LIVE: a projected carrier names this base AND a derived type is projected, so a derived value must be acceptable where the base is named. This is the only state that forces a public reference abstraction, and reaching it is a legitimate architecture stop

substitutabilityInventory.measured: 51 base-typed public signature positions across the twelve families. Three families -- GameComponent, GraphicsResource and MathTypeConverter -- are named in ZERO positions and carry 25 of the 41 derived types between them. Nine are LATENT. None is LIVE
substitutabilityInventory.closestToLive: Texture2D: 17 positions, nine of them on SpriteBatch, which CNA-Go projects. It stays LATENT only because its one derived type, RenderTarget2D, is not projected. Projecting RenderTarget2D while SpriteBatch.Draw takes a Texture2D is exactly what would make it live
substitutabilityInventory.crossCheck: the relationships the inventory walks are read from the contract's own baseType fields, never from this registry, and the two must agree exactly. A relationship in one and not the other is BASE_MAPPING_MISMATCH, so neither can go stale alone

compositionRule.projection: PRIVATE NAMED COMPOSITION plus EXPLICIT MEASURED FORWARDING. A derived XNA class holds its base in a private, named, pointer-typed field and declares every inherited public member itself
compositionRule.neverEmbedding: Go embedding is refused. It promotes the base's WHOLE method set, so a member the derived class overrides would silently keep the base's body wherever the derived one was not redeclared with exactly the right shape. Explicit forwarding makes every inherited member a declared, measured member of the derived type, so the override set is a fact the verifier checks rather than a property of Go's promotion rules
compositionRule.noBaseAccessor: no public Base, Parent, BaseObject, Inner, Super or As<Base> member. The pinned contract declares none, and Foundation 40 measured that no public signature in the profile needs one. An exported base field is refused for the same reason: it hands a consumer the base object and lets them mutate it behind the derived type's back
compositionRule.justification: Foundation 40's substitutability inventory. For a family named in ZERO public signature positions -- GameComponent, GraphicsResource and MathTypeConverter, 25 of the 41 derived types between them -- private composition is not a compromise but exactly sufficient: there is no position in the contract for a derived value to flow through
compositionRule.baseConstruction: a derived constructor creates its private base state at the exact CLR base-constructor point, preserving validation order, side effects, event subscription, reference identity and defaults. A field the derived class initializes BEFORE its base call in IL is initialized before it here too
compositionRule.overrides: a CLR virtual override projects as the derived Go method. A non-virtual base call -- `call Base::Member` -- invokes the private base state directly and must NOT redispatch; no public API is invented for internal base dispatch
compositionRule.consumerSubclassing: this rule projects Microsoft's OWN derived types. It does not attempt universal Go class inheritance for arbitrary consumer subclasses: Go cannot reproduce CLR subclassing, and the targeted language adapters that already exist -- GameCallbacks and the optional Game frame-hook capabilities -- remain the answer where consumer override behaviour is necessary

provenanceClasses.rule: every projected public member belongs to exactly ONE provenance class, so no member is ever counted twice and REFERENCE_MEMBERS keeps naming exactly what the Microsoft assemblies declare
provenanceClasses.XNA_DECLARED: the derived CLR type declares the member itself. 3243 Go projections of the 2,964 XNA-declared reference members; this number never moves
provenanceClasses.BCL_INHERITED: inherited directly or indirectly from a supported BCL base outside the contract, attributed to the exact base and the exact CLR member
provenanceClasses.XNA_INHERITED: inherited from another XNA contract class whose base relationship is COMPOSED, attributed the same way and walked transitively up the COMPOSED chain
provenanceClasses.overrideExclusion: a derived class that redeclares an inherited member is overriding or hiding it, so the projected member is the DERIVED one. Counting it in both classes would inflate the accounting and claim a forwarding that must not exist
provenanceClasses.constructorsAreNotInherited: CLR requires a derived class to declare its own, and every derived class in the profile does
provenanceClasses.protectedIsNotPublicSurface: a protected member is inherited in CLR but is not public surface, so it is not projected onto the derived type

gameNativeSignals.rule: Every projected XNA event Game declares must have its AUTHORITATIVE XNA raise path, and a canonical CNA signal may IMPLEMENT that path only when the semantics align. Three of the four events are raised by GameHost, whose part the native runtime plays, so for those three the signal IS the reference's raise path. The fourth is raised by managed Dispose(bool), so its raise is in Go and the signal is bound for lifetime qualification only
gameNativeSignals.noCNAChange: the four signals were already published by the pinned CNA C API and had never been reached from Go. Binding them added two bound functions to CNA-Go's manifest and changed no CNA C++, did not rebuild CNA, and did not alter the pinned artifact
gameNativeSignals.oneSubscriptionPerEvent: exactly one native subscription per event per Game, never one per consumer handler. CNA invokes multiple native registrations on one event in REVERSE registration order, measured against the pinned binary, so per-handler registration would invert the dispatch order the event projection promises
gameNativeSignals.subscriptionLifetime: installed on the owner thread immediately after cna_game_create, because CNA answers CNA_RESULT_THREAD for cna_game_subscribe from any other thread; released after cna_game_destroy, because the disposal signal is raised from inside that call and a registration handle stays valid across it; the cgo.Handle is deleted last, so a callback-after-free is unreachable
gameNativeSignals.errorBoundary: CNA_GameEventCallback returns void, so this boundary cannot stop the game -- the canonical header says these handlers only observe. A handler failure is recorded through the same callback-failure path every lifecycle failure uses and surfaces from Game.Run; a panic is recovered in the trampoline and recorded the same way. Nothing crosses the C frame and nothing is discarded
gameNativeSignals.ownerThread: every signal is delivered on the Game owner thread, measured. The projected accessors do not inherit that affinity: Add and Remove touch a mutex-guarded Go list and never reach C
gameNativeSignals.noNativeIdentity: CNA_GameEventRegistrationHandle, the cgo.Handle, the callback context pointer and the CNA_GAME_EVENT_* constants stay inside internal/interop. The public surface is EventHandler[*EventArgs] and EventSubscription, exactly as for every other projected XNA event

senders.GAME: the raise pushes `ldarg.0`, which is the Game itself and NOT the sender parameter the On... method was handed
senders.NULL: the raise pushes `ldnull`. Game::OnExiting is the only member of this family that does, and it is observable from every handler

runtimeEvidence.VERIFIED_NATIVE: the qualification artifact actually delivers the signal, and the delivery is counted. Such a signal records no evidence reason: an excuse next to a verification means the label and the evidence disagree
runtimeEvidence.NOT_RUN_ENVIRONMENT: the environment cannot produce the signal. A reason is REQUIRED, and the delivery counter is left at zero rather than made to move

gameNativeSignals.ruleSupersedes: the Foundation 34 rule was 'every event is bound to exactly one canonical signal, through exactly the raise path the reference uses'. That is satisfied by binding a signal to an event whose reference raise site is not the host's at all, which is the divergence it shipped for Game::Disposed: the native signal fires from cna_game_destroy, so it fired for a consumer who never disposed anything and did not fire for one who disposed without ever running. Foundation 39 projects Dispose and corrects it

raisePath.NATIVE_HOST_SIGNAL: the canonical CNA signal drives the raise, because the reference's raise path is GameHost's and the native runtime plays GameHost's part
raisePath.MANAGED: the reference raises the event from managed code CNA-Go projects, so the raise is in Go and the native signal must not drive it. A managed raise path must name the projected protected member that raises it

nativeSignalRole.PUBLIC_EVENT_RAISE: the bound signal drives the projected event
nativeSignalRole.LIFECYCLE_ONLY: the bound signal is delivered and counted for native lifetime qualification and raises nothing public. It stays bound because it is what proves a registration outlives cna_game_destroy

gameNativeSignals.raisePathAndRolePairing: one decision seen from two ends: NATIVE_HOST_SIGNAL pairs with PUBLIC_EVENT_RAISE and MANAGED pairs with LIFECYCLE_ONLY. A signal cannot drive an event the reference raises somewhere else, and an event the host really raises cannot have a signal that raises nothing
gameNativeSignals.nativeSignalMoment: what the CNA signal actually means, recorded for every signal. For a LIFECYCLE_ONLY role it is the statement of WHY the semantics do not align, so the divergence is a measured fact rather than a comment

gameFrameHooks.rule: Game's four frame-boundary protected virtuals project as METHODS ON Game, because the mapper redirects exactly the five protected virtuals GameCallbacks declares and no others. Each records the canonical CNA hook that sits at the same frame position, WHEN CNA-Go installs it, and -- for a hook installed behind an override -- the unexported single-method Go interface a consumer satisfies to opt in
theseAreNot: GameCallbacks members: the mandatory override contract keeps exactly its five members, and adding to it would break every existing external implementation

base-call adapters: the GameBase... registry is keyed by the GameCallbacks members, so GameBaseBeginRun and friends are exactly the invented helpers its closure rule stops. The projected methods on Game ARE the base bodies, so an override reaches its base by calling game.BeginDraw() and needs no helper
exported capability contracts: the four optional overrides are discovered structurally through UNEXPORTED single-method interfaces, so the mechanism publishes no new public framework identity

registration APIs: there is no Set..., Register... or Add...Override anywhere. A consumer opts in by declaring the method, the capability is captured once in NewGame, and no exported member or type in the framework package may be named ...Override
gameFrameHooks.beginDrawBoolean: the Boolean is a value channel, not a success flag. DrawFrame runs `if (BeginDraw()) { Draw(); EndDraw(); }`, so false skips both, and the measured native hook does the same: a frame whose out_should_draw is CNA_FALSE delivers neither draw nor end_draw. The Boolean is never collapsed into the error -- a refusal is (false, nil) and is never promoted to a failure, and a failing override leaves the runtime's own drawing decision untouched rather than turning the failure into a refusal
gameFrameHooks.graphicsDeviceManager: Game::graphicsDeviceManager has one assignment in the whole class, at the head of RunGame, and the statement after it calls CreateDevice on what it found. The native CNA runtime owns and creates the device, and Foundation 30 audited that the projected GraphicsDeviceManager satisfies neither service contract, so the reference's only registrar cannot run. The field is permanently null, which is a state the reference itself has whenever no manager is registered; both draw bodies are reproduced as written and the null branch is the one always taken
gameFrameHooks.deferredSteps: same classes and same rule as the base-call adapters: SUBSYSTEM, ARCHITECTURE or UNOBSERVABLE, each with a reason, and a deferral marked observable is REJECTED as a stop condition

installation.NEVER: the canonical native hook is not installed at all. A reason is REQUIRED
installation.ON_OVERRIDE: the canonical native hook is installed if and only if the callback object handed to NewGame supplies the matching optional override. With no override the CNA_GameFrameHooks member stays NULL, which the canonical header defines as simply not called, so the native frame position behaves exactly as it did before the mechanism existed

gameFrameHooks.capabilities: one unexported single-method Go interface per hook, never one bundled contract. A CLR subclass may override any SUBSET of the four virtuals, and a consumer forced to supply a no-op for a virtual they did not override would be installing a hook that takes the base's place. Every capability method takes the owning Game -- the `this` a CLR base call passes implicitly -- and returns exactly what the base body it replaces returns. The interfaces are unexported because Go interfaces are structural: a consumer declares the exported method and never names the type
gameFrameHooks.baseCalls: inside an override, calling the corresponding method on the Game is the Go projection of base.BeginRun(), base.EndRun(), base.BeginDraw() or base.EndDraw(). Zero calls means the base does not run, one call runs it once at that source position, and two calls run it twice; nothing deduplicates or suppresses a repeated explicit call. The call site is the semantics, exactly as it is in CLR. Those methods read only Game's own state and never consult the callback object, so an explicit base call cannot re-enter the override
gameFrameHooks.discovery: exactly once, in NewGame, at the same boundary where GameCallbacks itself becomes associated with the Game. A Go object's method set is fixed for its whole lifetime, so a later re-check could not produce a different answer and there is nothing to mutate; the captured capabilities are private fields and no frame pays for a type assertion
gameFrameHooks.noThirdInstallationClass: there is no ALWAYS. An unconditionally installed hook would run a base body at a frame position CNA-Go picked and make that base call mandatory, which is exactly what Foundation 31 settled against, so it is not a class this registry can express and declaring one is an unclassified installation

baseInvocation.EXPLICIT_ONLY: the base body runs only where the override's own source calls the method on the Game, zero, one or many times. It is the only admitted class, and every hook must record how it is known

blockedDeclaredMembers.rule: a member a pinned XNA type DECLARES that CNA-Go does not project, with the exact external closure that blocks it. It is the declared-member counterpart of a base adapter's BCL_PROJECTION_BLOCKED_EXTERNAL exclusion and carries the same weight: an admission, not a permission
blockedDeclaredMembers.measured: the identity must name a member the pinned contract really declares; the entry must state its kind, what it needs and why; and the count is reported as BLOCKED_DECLARED_MEMBERS, separately from MISSING_MEMBER

entries.Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Content.ContentL: BCL_PROJECTION_BLOCKED_EXTERNAL: a protected deserialization constructor whose two parameter types are the serialization closure Foundation 74 measured; its only CLR caller is a formatter, and CNA-Go deserialises nothing
entries.Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Storage.StorageD: the same protected deserialization constructor on the other type that declares one
